did_you_know.text: Solomon married Pharaoh’s daughter and initially brought her to the City of David. She remained there until he finished building his palace, the house of the LORD, and the wall around Jerusalem.

During Solomon’s reign, the people were still offering sacrifices at the high places because the temple of the LORD had not yet been built. This chapter does not say that every sacrifice offered at a high place was unacceptable at that time.
Gibeon is described as the “great high place.” There Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings on the altar, before the dream in which the LORD appeared to him.
At Gibeon, the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream and said, “Ask for whatever you want me to give you.” This gave Solomon the opportunity to ask the LORD for a gift.
Solomon did not ask first of all for wealth or victory over his enemies, but for a “listening heart”—the ability to distinguish between good and evil and to judge the people fairly.
Solomon’s request pleased the LORD precisely because he had asked for understanding to administer justice, rather than asking for long life, wealth, or the lives of his enemies.
The LORD promised Solomon a wise and discerning heart, describing his wisdom as unparalleled both before him and after him.
Wealth and honor were promised to Solomon, while long life was made conditional on his walking in the LORD’s ways and keeping his laws and commands.
After waking and realizing that it had been a dream, Solomon returned to Jerusalem, stood before the ark of the LORD’s covenant, offered sacrifices, and held a feast for all his servants.

In the judgment involving the two women, Solomon did not truly intend to have the child divided. His proposal revealed the response of the mother who wanted to save the child’s life. As a result, all Israel recognized the divine wisdom within him.
